newsitem.title: USA: Big nations again urge stable dollar, to no avail.
newsitem.headline: Big nations again urge stable dollar, to no avail.

text.p: Major industrial nations backed their call for currency stability with more words but no action on Monday as the dollar climbed further on world foreign exchange markets.
"We do not want overshoot (in curency rates)," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer told reporters ahead of a meeting of the International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee here.

But the markets did not seem to pay much attention. The dollar briefly rose to a 37-month high against the German mark and to near its 55-month peak against the Japanese yen on Monday, before settling back at the close of New York trading, where it closed above 1.73 marks and just shy of 127 yen.

In a communique issued on Sunday after five hours of talks, the Group of Seven industrial nations called for stability in currency markets and warned against rate swings that could lead to trade problems down the road.

"We agreed that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility and significant deviations from fundamentals are undesirable," the finance ministers and central bank chiefs from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States said.

The United States and Japan in particular seem concerned about the dollar's relentless rise against the yen -- it has appreciated by more than 50 percent over the past two years -- and the impact that could have on world commerce.
The dollar's climb against the yen has given Japanese exporters an advantage over their U.S. rivals on world markets, threatening to throw trade between the two nations further out of whack.
To help curb the dollar's rise and head off friction with the United States, Japanese officials have hinted that major nations might step in the currency market to sell greenbacks.
But so far such intervention has not occured. And there is some question about how effective such action would be now.
"It's hard for the G7 to stop the dollar on basis of economic fundamentals, which are still very positive," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.

With U.S. interest rates high and rising and Japanese interest rates low and stable, many investors see little reason now to sell their dollars for yen -- no matter what long-term impact those currency rates may have on trade flows.

Bank of England Governor Eddie George, while saying that he was not completely comfortable with the large currency gyrations that have occured in the past, neverthless cautioned major nations against promising more than they could deliver.
"Frustrating though it is, we should be cautious in promising greater exchange rate stability than we can deliver," George told the IMF Interim Committee.

For his part, IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus envinced little concern about the current constellation of currency rates. "Exchange rates among the major currencies are generally consistent with broader policy objectives," he said.
Although the strong dollar could spell trade difficulties for the United States in the future, for now it is acting as an important check on inflation by keeping down import prices.

Policymakers attending the IMF meeting from European nations generally seemed more preoccupied with their planned launch of a single currency in 1999 than they did with recent movements on the exchange market.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told the Interim Committee that the new currency -- to be called the euro -- would be a stabilising force in the world monetary system.
"The euro is coming soon -- on January 1, 1999 it will be a reality. We are ready," he said. "The euro will be a stabilising force in the European Union and the international monetary system."
And Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi repeated his belief that Italy will meet the tough budget targets required to join European monetary union in 1999.
